sections.title: Why are Plant and Animal Tissues Different?
Apical meristem: How do plants grow in length?
Lateral meristem: How do plants grow in girth?
Intercalary meristem: How do plants grow after being cut?

slides.title: Fixed Roots, Moving Feet
slides.kicker: Why plants stand still and animals roam
bullets: Most plants are fixed in one place and do not move about, so they need support to stay firm and upright.
Plant cells have a cell wall that provides rigidity and strength.
Animals can generally move; without a rigid cell wall their cells can change shape easily.
This cellular flexibility helps make animal bodies suitable for locomotion, though some animals like sponges are immobile.

right.title: Animals
items: Mostly move from place to place

slides.note: Cell wall ki wajah plant pakka khada, animal full flexible!

slides.title: Two Ways of Feeding
slides.kicker: Sunlight kitchen versus food hunting
bullets: Plants have tissues that utilise solar energy for synthesising food components through photosynthesis.
Animals have tissues that help them digest food obtained from different food sources.
Plants and animals also have distinct tissues for transporting food and water to different parts of the body.

slides.title: Structure Suits Function
slides.kicker: The one idea this whole chapter builds
bullets: Growth patterns in plants and animals vary because the tissues responsible for growth differ in structure and function.
In this chapter we learn how the structures of plant and animal tissues relate to their specific functions.
Meet a Scientist: B.G.L. Swamy, expert in plant morphology and anatomy, won the Kendra Sahitya Akademi award in 1978.
slides.note: Ek hi funda baar baar: jo shape, wahi kaam.

slides.title: A Seedling's Promise
slides.kicker: Small seed today, tall tree tomorrow
bullets: A small seedling grows into a tall tree and its roots grow deep into the soil.
Stems become thicker with time, and grass grows again after being eaten by grazing animals.
The big question: which tissues are responsible for these changes?

slides.title: Three Ways to Grow
slides.kicker: Length, girth, and a comeback
bullets: Increase in length means height of the stem and depth of the roots.
Increase in girth means thickness of the stem.
Regrowth means growing again after cutting the branches or grazing by animals.

slides.title: Meet the Meristematic Tissue
slides.kicker: Dividing cells are the growth engine
bullets: Growth in plants requires actively dividing cells.
These actively dividing cells together form a tissue called meristematic tissue.
Plants have different kinds of meristematic tissues, one for each growth job.

slides.title: The Two Jar Experiment
slides.kicker: Onion bulbs settle a growing debate
bullets: Take two glass jars filled with water and place one onion bulb in each.
Observe root growth and measure root lengths on days 1, 2 and 3.
On day 3, cut the root tips of the onion bulb in Jar B by about 1 cm, then measure lengths for four more days.

items: Cut Jar B root tips by 1 cm

slides.title: What the Jars Showed
slides.kicker: Cut the tip, stop the growth
bullets: Roots in Jar A continue to grow in length through the experiment.
Roots in Jar B stop growing after the tips are cut.
This shows that roots grow only from their tips, which consist of cells that divide continuously.
slides.note: Tip katao toh lambai ruk jaati hai, seedha proof!

slides.title: Apical Meristem at Work
slides.kicker: Growth zones hiding at every tip
bullets: Observing mitosis in onion root tips, as done in Chapter 2, confirms that root tips contain actively dividing cells.
Shoot tips also contain actively dividing cells that help the shoots grow in length.
Plants have growth zones at the tips of roots and shoots called apical meristems, which help plants grow in length.

slides.title: Rings That Tell Time
slides.kicker: A trunk's diary carved in wood
bullets: A cut trunk seen at a timber yard shows ring-like patterns called annual growth rings.
Some annual rings are wide and some are narrow, reflecting favourable or unfavourable growth conditions during a particular year.
By counting these annual rings, scientists can estimate the age of a tree and understand the climatic conditions under which it grew.

slides.title: Girth Needs a Ring
slides.kicker: Dividing cells circle the stem
bullets: Increase in girth occurs due to actively dividing cells arranged in a ring in the stem.
These cells divide and produce new cells inside and outside in a concentric manner.
The result is an increase in the diameter of the stem.

items: New cells form inside and outside

slides.title: Lateral Meristem Defined
slides.kicker: Dicot stems widen year by year
bullets: Stems of dicot plants grow in length and also increase in diameter or girth over time.
One possible explanation for this increase is the activity of meristematic tissues.
This ring-shaped meristematic tissue is called the lateral meristem.

slides.title: Cut Tip, New Branches
slides.kicker: Pruning wakes up sleepy nodes
bullets: If the tip of a young stem is cut, the stem stops growing in length.
New branches then arise from the nodes of the stem.
The intercalary meristem is located at the base of internode or just above the node.

slides.title: Hedges and Mowed Grass
slides.kicker: The bushy comeback trick
bullets: When a garden hedge is cut, more branches appear after some time, giving the hedge a bushy appearance.
Grass also appears again after being mowed or grazed by animals.
This regrowth happens because of intercalary meristem at the nodes of the grass stem.

slides.title: Three Meristems, One Team
slides.kicker: Length, girth and regrowth settled
bullets: The apical meristem, located at the root and shoot tips, increases length.
The lateral meristem, located along the circumference of stems, increases girth.
The intercalary meristem, located at the base of certain plants such as grasses, helps them regenerate after cutting.
slides.note: Teen meristem milke poora plant grow karte hain.

slides.title: Inside a Dividing Cell
slides.kicker: Built for speed, built for division
bullets: Meristematic cells are small, have thin cell walls, a large and prominent nucleus, and dense cytoplasm with many organelles.
Vacuoles are generally absent, and the cells are tightly packed with little or no intercellular space.
These characteristics allow continuous and rapid cell division.

slides.title: From Meristem to Permanent
slides.kicker: When dividing cells pick a career
bullets: Meristematic tissue keeps adding new cells; some stay meristematic while others lose the ability to divide.
Cells that lose the ability to divide change in structure and function, and become permanent tissues.
They become specialised for support, transport or storage; this process is called differentiation.

slides.title: Permanent Tissues Appear
slides.kicker: A stem slice under the microscope
bullets: A transverse section of a sunflower stem shows different groups of cells, each tissue specialised to perform a specific function.
These specialised groups of cells are permanent tissues.
Permanent tissues can be simple, composed of only one type of cell, or complex, composed of more than one type of cell.

left.title: Simple
items: Made of only one type of cell

right.title: Complex
items: Made of more than one type of cell

slides.title: Epidermis, the Shield
slides.kicker: One tight layer guards the plant
bullets: The epidermis forms the outermost layer of the plant body, protecting all its parts.
It consists of a tightly packed, single layer of flat and rectangular cells.
A waxy layer of cutin called the cuticle covers the cells, reducing water loss and guarding against injury and parasites.

slides.title: Stomata and Root Hairs
slides.kicker: Two tiny doors, two big jobs
bullets: In leaves, the epidermis has pores called stomata for gaseous exchange and transpiration, the evaporation of water vapours.
Transpiration creates a pull in the xylem that helps water transport and removes wastes.
In roots, hair-like projections called root hairs increase the surface area for absorption of water and minerals from the soil.
slides.note: Stomata se paani bhi bhaagta hai, gas bhi aati jaati hai.

slides.title: Supporting Tissues Begin
slides.kicker: Fresh twigs bend, dry twigs break
bullets: Supporting tissues carry functions like keeping a plant upright, hard seed coats and floating aquatic plants.
There are three types of supporting tissues or simple permanent tissues; the book names parenchyma and collenchyma among them.
Parenchyma consists of living cells with thin walls, loosely packed with intercellular spaces.

slides.title: Your Body Is Busy Now
slides.kicker: Blink, breathe, clench, feel
bullets: Blink your eyes quickly, clench and open your fist, take a deep breath, touch something warm or cold.
Each action asks a question: which tissue helps you move, sense heat or cold, let oxygen enter the blood, or hold the body together?
The answers lie in the diversity of animal tissues, which are specially adapted to perform different functions.

slides.title: Cells That Team Up
slides.kicker: Similar cells, one shared mission
bullets: Like plants, animal cells also group together and specialise in performing different functions.
These groups of similar cells form animal tissues.
Each animal tissue performs a specific function.

slides.title: Structure Suits Function
slides.kicker: Same question, animal edition
bullets: Animal tissues are specially adapted to perform different functions.
It is interesting to understand how the structure of an animal tissue suits its specific function.
First stop on the tour: epithelial tissue, the body's own covering and lining.

slides.title: The Body's Cover Story
slides.kicker: Skin outside, linings inside
bullets: Epithelial tissue forms the outer covering of the body, the skin.
It also lines the internal organs, such as the mouth, lungs, blood vessels and intestine.
One tissue works at two stations: the outside cover and the inner linings.

slides.title: Packed Tight for Safety
slides.kicker: No gaps, no entry for germs
bullets: Epithelial tissue is composed of closely packed cells with very little space between them.
This structure prevents the entry of germs and reduces water loss.
It also helps in the absorption, secretion and movement of substances.

slides.title: One Tissue, Many Shapes
slides.kicker: Structure and function paired up
bullets: Different types of epithelial tissues are structurally adapted to perform different functions.
Receptor epithelial cells found in the nostrils, taste buds and inner ear handle sensations like taste.
A single layer of tall, pillar-like cells, often hair-like, lines the small intestine for absorbing nutrients and water.

flashcards.front: What makes plant cells rigid but animal cells flexible?
flashcards.back: Plant cells have a cell wall that provides rigidity and strength. Animal cells lack it, so they can change shape easily.

flashcards.front: How do plants and animals get their food differently?
flashcards.back: Plant tissues utilise solar energy to synthesise food by photosynthesis, while animals have tissues to digest food from different sources.

flashcards.front: Which Indian scientist studied plant morphology and anatomy?
flashcards.back: B.G.L. Swamy, honoured with the Kendra Sahitya Akademi award in 1978 for his popular Kannada book describing plants of the Western Ghats.

flashcards.front: Which tissue powers all growth in plants?
flashcards.back: Meristematic tissue, made of actively dividing cells.

flashcards.front: Name the three ways plants grow.
flashcards.back: Increase in length (height of stem and depth of roots), increase in girth (thickness of stem), and regrowth after cutting or grazing.

flashcards.front: Give one everyday sign of plant regrowth.
flashcards.back: Grass grows again after grazing animals eat it, and a hedge turns bushy some time after trimming.

flashcards.front: What did the onion jar experiment prove?
flashcards.back: Jar A roots kept growing while Jar B roots stopped after the tips were cut, so roots grow only from their tips.

flashcards.front: Where is the apical meristem and what does it do?
flashcards.back: It sits at the tips of roots and shoots; its continuously dividing cells help the plant grow in length.

flashcards.front: Which cell process was seen in onion root tips in Chapter 2?
flashcards.back: Mitosis, which confirms that root tips contain actively dividing cells.

flashcards.front: What are annual growth rings?
flashcards.back: Ring-like patterns on the cut surface of wood; wide rings reflect favourable growth conditions and narrow rings unfavourable ones that year.

flashcards.front: How can scientists estimate a tree's age?
flashcards.back: By counting annual growth rings on the cut trunk; the rings also reveal the climatic conditions under which the tree grew.

flashcards.front: Define lateral meristem.
flashcards.back: Actively dividing cells arranged in a ring in the stem; they produce new cells inside and outside, increasing the girth.

flashcards.front: What happens when the tip of a young stem is cut?
flashcards.back: The stem stops growing in length, but new branches arise from the nodes of the stem.

flashcards.front: Distinguish node and internode.
flashcards.back: A node is the point on the stem where branches or leaves arise; the internode is the part of stem between two nodes.

flashcards.front: Why does mowed grass grow back?
flashcards.back: Intercalary meristem at the nodes of its stem helps grass regenerate after cutting or grazing.

flashcards.front: List three traits of meristematic cells.
flashcards.back: Small cells with thin walls, a large prominent nucleus and dense cytoplasm; vacuoles generally absent; tightly packed with little or no intercellular space.

flashcards.front: What is differentiation in plants?
flashcards.back: The process by which meristematic tissue loses the ability to divide and becomes permanent tissue specialised for specific functions.

flashcards.front: Simple versus complex permanent tissue?
flashcards.back: Simple permanent tissue is composed of only one type of cell; complex permanent tissue is composed of more than one type of cell.

flashcards.front: What is the cuticle made of and what does it do?
flashcards.back: A waxy layer of cutin covering epidermal cells; it reduces water loss and protects against mechanical injury and invasion by parasites.

flashcards.front: How do root hairs and stomata serve the plant?
flashcards.back: Root hairs increase surface area for absorbing water and minerals; stomata allow gaseous exchange and transpiration.

flashcards.front: Describe parenchyma cells.
flashcards.back: Living cells with thin walls, loosely packed with intercellular spaces.

flashcards.front: What forms an animal tissue?
flashcards.back: Groups of similar animal cells that group together and specialise to perform a specific function.

flashcards.front: Name four quick actions that reveal animal tissues at work.
flashcards.back: Blinking your eyes, clenching and opening your fist, taking a deep breath, and touching something warm or cold.

flashcards.front: What big question guides the study of animal tissues?
flashcards.back: How the structure of an animal tissue suits its specific function.

flashcards.front: Where does epithelial tissue occur in the body?
flashcards.back: It forms the outer covering of the body (skin) and lines internal organs such as the mouth, lungs, blood vessels and intestine.

flashcards.front: Which jobs does epithelial tissue do besides protection?
flashcards.back: It helps in absorption, secretion and movement of substances.

flashcards.front: Which epithelial cells handle taste and sensing?
flashcards.back: Receptor cells found in the nostrils, taste buds and inner ear.

examples.title: Predict the onion jar results
examples.problem: In Activity 3.1, two onion bulbs sit in two jars of water. On day 3, the Jar A root measures 20 mm and the Jar B root measures 18 mm, and then the root tips of Jar B are cut by about 1 cm. Predict the readings from day 4 to day 7 and explain your prediction.
steps: Recall the experiment conclusion: roots grow only from their tips, which consist of cells that divide continuously.
Jar A keeps its tips, so its dividing cells keep adding length and the root grows a little more each day beyond 20 mm.
Jar B lost its root tips on day 3, so the actively dividing cells were removed and the root stays at about 18 mm.
Compare with Table 3.1 of the book: only the jar with intact tips shows rising readings after day 3.
examples.answer: Jar A keeps growing beyond 20 mm, while Jar B stops at about 18 mm, proving that root tips hold the apical meristem that grows roots in length.

examples.title: Read a tree's life from its rings
examples.problem: The cut trunk of a tree seen at a timber yard shows 40 annual growth rings, of which 26 are wide and 14 are narrow. What can you conclude about the tree's age and the conditions it grew in?
steps: Each ring-like pattern on the cut surface is an annual growth ring, so 40 rings mean about 40 years of growth.
Wide rings reflect favourable growth conditions during that particular year.
Narrow rings reflect unfavourable growth conditions during that particular year.
So 26 of its 40 years were favourable for growth and 14 years were unfavourable.
examples.answer: The tree was about 40 years old, with 26 favourable years (wide rings) and 14 unfavourable years (narrow rings); the rings also reveal the climatic conditions under which it grew.

examples.title: Match each job to its tissue
examples.problem: Classify these plant parts and events: (a) a root growing deeper into the soil, (b) an old dicot trunk growing thicker, (c) mowed grass sprouting again, (d) the outermost layer of a sunflower stem guarding it, (e) loosely packed living cells with thin walls inside the stem.
steps: (a) Growth in depth happens at the root tip, so the apical meristem is at work.
(b) A widening trunk shows actively dividing cells arranged in a ring, so the lateral meristem is at work.
(c) Regrowth after cutting points to the intercalary meristem at the nodes of grass.
(d) The outermost single layer of flat rectangular cells with a waxy cuticle is the epidermis, a protective tissue.
(e) Living, thin-walled, loosely packed cells with intercellular spaces describe parenchyma, a simple permanent tissue.
examples.answer: (a) apical meristem, (b) lateral meristem, (c) intercalary meristem, (d) epidermis, (e) parenchyma

steps.label: Why tissues differ
steps.detail: Plants are fixed with cell walls; animals move with flexible cells.

steps.label: Meristematic tissue
steps.detail: Actively dividing cells power all plant growth.

steps.label: Apical meristem
steps.detail: The onion jar experiment shows tips grow roots in length.

steps.label: Lateral meristem
steps.detail: A ring of dividing cells adds girth; annual rings record the years.

steps.label: Intercalary meristem
steps.detail: Nodes of grass and hedges regrow after cutting.

steps.label: Differentiation
steps.detail: Some new cells stop dividing and specialise for specific jobs.

steps.label: Permanent tissues
steps.detail: Epidermis protects the plant; simple tissues like parenchyma support it.

steps.label: Animal tissues
steps.detail: Similar cells team up; epithelial tissue covers and lines the body.
